title: Cachekey ontology, TTL sandboxing, and shadow-apply rollout
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Implement a judged, sandbox-first flow for generating prefix/key recommendations, testing TTL skews under realistic workloads, and applying changes via a shadow/staged apply with automatic rollback triggers. This ticket covers: cache-key ontology (grouping and canonicalization), a TTL sandbox that runs counterfactual simulations, a shadow-apply harness for safe prod evaluation, and automated rollback logic driven by hit-rate and latency regressions.
background: We have recurrent opportunities to reduce tokens and GPU cycles by improving per-prefix KV TTLs and cache key canonicalization. Past manual rollouts have led to transient tail-latency regressions during high-burst windows (incidents documented in ENG-384900-incident-postmortem). Teams need an automated, low-risk way to validate policy changes against live traffic distributions before committing them.
goals: Produce a stable cachekey ontology that reduces artificial key cardinality and improves per-prefix hit rates
Provide TTL recommendation engine outputs (per-prefix suggested TTL range and confidence) from sandboxed simulations
Enable shadow-apply in production to measure hit-rate/latency/cost delta without affecting actual reads/writes
Ship an automated rollout + rollback policy that reverts changes when hit-rate or p99 latency cross thresholds
Document runbook and integrate metrics into Console dashboards and alerts
scope: Design and implement cachekey normalization heuristics (affix stripping, tokenization rules, tenant-aware bucketing)
TTL recommendation engine that consumes prefix access traces and synthetic replay workloads
Sandbox service to run counterfactuals (simulate TTL changes) and estimate hit-rate impact and eviction pressure
Shadow-apply service: write-intent tagging and sidecar metrics collection; no client-visible cache effects
Automated rollback controller with configurable thresholds and audit logging
success_metrics: Verified end-to-end workflow (recommendation -> shadow -> canary -> apply) demonstrated on internal prod canary tenant
>= 6% token-cost reduction on the canary tenant under typical weekly traffic (measured over two 7-day windows)
No >10% increase in p99 inference latency during full shadow window; automatic rollback kicks in if exceeded
Documentation and runbook published and reviewed by SRE, Platform, and Product
Two engineers trained on runbook and able to perform manual emergency rollback in <10 minutes
design_decisions: Canonicalization: use affix-aware rules plus a tenant-aware suffix to preserve multi-tenant isolation; avoid lossy hashing for high-variance prefixes
TTL recommendation: emit a range with a confidence score (low/medium/high) using bootstrap simulations rather than a single point estimate
Shadow-apply approach: writes will be tagged and duplicated to a shadow cache namespace; reads remain unchanged unless canary mode is explicitly enabled
Rollback triggers: combine both absolute thresholds (e.g., p99 latency delta > 10%) and statistical tests on hit-rate drop (95% CI) to avoid noisy reverts

Batching considerations: when increasing TTLs, coordinate with batching config because larger TTLs may increase effective cache reuse and allow more aggressive batching without increasing tail latency
tradeoffs: Aggressive canonicalization reduces cardinality but risks key collisions that bias hit-rate estimates; we will mitigate via collision metrics and staged rollouts
Long TTLs decrease upstream calls but increase memory/ejection pressure on cache nodes during bursts; sandbox sim will quantify eviction risk
Shadow-apply adds write amplification and monitoring overhead; we accept this cost for a limited shadow window to gain safety guarantees
Confidence-based recommendations are conservative by default; this reduces immediate savings but lowers rollback frequency and operational toil
rollout_plan: 1) Internal dry-run: run sandbox simulations on replay of last 14 days of traffic (no prod interaction). Validate recommendation outputs against historical hit-rate.
2) Shadow window: enable shadow-apply for a small set of low-risk tenants (canary tenancy group) for 72h. Collect metrics: shadow-hit, shadow-evictions, write-amplification, p50/p95/p99 latencies.
3) Canary apply (read-only): enable canary reads for 5% of traffic with feature flag and monitor for 48h
4) Gradual rollout: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 7 days with automated checks at each step
5) Full apply and cleanup: retire shadow namespaces and update Console recommendations and docs
rollback_playbook: Automated: controller observes metric breach and flips feature flag back to previous mapping within 30s; records audit event and triggers PagerDuty if p99 latency spike > 20%
Manual: operators can trigger 'force-rollback' endpoint which re-applies last known-good TTL map and rehydrates critical prefixes from snapshot
Emergency: if controller is unhealthy, operators follow emergency procedure (docs link) to disable shadowing globally and restore previous policy map
Post-rollback: run a forensics job to compute root cause (eviction curves, collision traces) and open follow-up ticket with remediation
monitoring_and_alerts: New Grafana dashboard: KV TTL rollout scorecard (shadow_hit_rate, delta_hit_rate, eviction_rate, p99_latency_delta, write_amplification)
Alert: p99_delta > 10% for 5 minutes -> warning; > 15% for 2 minutes -> critical (auto-rollback)
Alert: shadow_eviction_rate > baseline * 2 for 10 minutes -> investigate (no auto-rollback, operator review)
Audit logs: every TTL map change must be recorded with actor, commit hash, and sandbox report link
test_plan: Unit tests for canonicalization heuristics and collision detection
Integration tests for sandbox replay harness using synthetic prefixes (bursty, long-tail, tenant-mix)
Load tests: run shadow-apply under 2x peak traffic to validate monitoring and write amplification handling
Canary regression tests: verify no user-visible latency regression for read-only canary before enabling writes
Chaos test: simulate a cache node restart during rollout and validate rollback path keeps system stable
open_questions: What is the acceptable per-tenant memory budget increase during a rollout (SRE input needed)?
Should canonicalization rules be configurable per-org or globally applied?
Do we allow operator overrides for TTL suggestions in Console or restrict changes to programmatic pipelines?
Edge-case: how to handle prefixes with highly multimodal sequence lengths that cause KV cache fragmentation?
